title: Recalibrating Africa’s green hydrogen strategy, Part 3
body:
Hydrogen (H2) roadmaps are emerging across African countries, most of them led by energy ministries, climate agencies, and investment promotion units. The emphasis is typically on production capacity, export terminals, and offtake agreements.

This pattern raises an uncomfortable question: what if African countries are designing H2 policy as if it were LNG 2.0?

The answer is familiar:

- Large-scale projects move fast. Export terminals are built. Foreign buyers sign long-term contracts. H2 molecules leave African ports.
- 10-15 years from now, Africa becomes most likely a competitive exporter of green molecules. GDP rises modestly. Government revenues increase.
- However, industrial structures will remain largely unchanged. Electrolyzers are imported. Engineering services are foreign-led. Steel and fertilizer industries remain underdeveloped.

Result: high investment, with little or no structural transformation. Africa’s H2 moment MUST BECOME MUCH MORE THAN THIS.

Breaking free from the supposedly “Export enclave path” requires coordinated governance—an argument I have highlighted more broadly in an earlier policy insight (https://lnkd.in/eR7i6VqN).

In H2 context, this requires energy ministries to design H2 supply but in lockstep where:

- Ministries of Industry shape downstream strategies: green steel, fertilizers, chemicals, synthetic fuels.
- Ministries of Trade integrate H2-based products into export competitiveness strategies and AfCFTA frameworks.
- Ministries of Agriculture link green ammonia production to fertilizer security and agro-industrial clusters.
- Finance ministries and development banks must design instruments that support industrial parks, supplier development, and technology upgrading — not just production facilities..

The implication of this “coordinated industrial path” is clear:

- Export contracts are negotiated, but include downstream investment commitments.
- H2 zones are co-located with industrial clusters.
- Skill systems are aligned early and local firms are integrated into fabrication, maintenance, storage, and component manufacturing.

H2 is not simply a molecule or an export project. It is a potential anchor for industrial ecosystem. What determines whether it fulfills this purpose is “GOVERNANCE”.

Without deliberate coordination, H2 risks becoming an export commodity. With coordination, it becomes a structural transformation lever.

Africa’s H2 can therefore become another export corridor or a platform for green industrialization. The choice is institutional, and the window is open now.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D.
